title: How do restaurants and fast-food chains make money, and what matters in their cases?
description: Restaurant economics for case interviews: covers, average spend, food and labour costs, franchising and delivery apps, with a worked unit-economics example.
hook: Restaurants make money by serving enough customers at a high enough average spend to cover food, labour and rent, which together swallow most of every dollar; chains then grow either by opening their own sites or by franchising and collecting royalties. Restaurant cases test unit economics: what one restaurant earns and costs, whether that holds at the next site, and what delivery apps and franchising do to the numbers.
body:
The basic equation

Revenue = covers (customers served) × average spend. Covers depend on seats, opening hours and how many times each table turns over; average spend depends on menu prices and what people add. The biggest costs are usually food and packaging and labour, which operators often track together as "prime cost", followed by rent. Utilities, marketing, repairs and card fees make up the rest.

A worked example: one restaurant's profit

An illustrative fast-casual restaurant serves 400 customers a day at $10 each, 360 days a year.

LineShare of salesAmount
Revenue100%$1.44M
Food and packaging30%$432k
Labour30%$432k
Rent and other costs25%$360k
Restaurant profit15%$216k

If the restaurant cost $600k to fit out, payback is $600k ÷ $216k ≈ 2.8 years. That single-site model is the foundation of every chain case. Before discussing expansion, check whether it holds at the next site: a busy flagship near offices may not predict sales in a suburb with different lunch traffic.

Notice the sensitivity. Food plus labour is 60% of sales. A three-point rise in labour costs, from 30% to 33%, cuts profit from 15% to 12% of sales, a fifth of the restaurant's profit.

Franchising

Many chains let franchisees own and run most restaurants, paying the chain an upfront fee and a royalty on sales. McDonald's is the classic example: about 95% of its US restaurants are franchised. The chain earns far less per restaurant than if it owned it, but needs very little capital and takes less risk, so it can grow much faster. At an illustrative 5% royalty, the restaurant above pays the chain $72k a year, against $216k of profit if the chain owned it, but without the $600k investment. See how businesses make money for the wider model.

Delivery apps

Apps bring orders but charge a commission on every order, and some of their orders are customers who would have ordered directly anyway. Say a restaurant gets $120k a year of app orders, half of which replace orders it used to take directly. The truly new revenue is $60k. Food and packaging on that new revenue at 32% is $19.2k, and a 25% commission on the full $120k is $30k. The gain is $60k − $19.2k − $30k = $10.8k, before any extra staff time. A channel that looks like $120k of growth adds about $11k of profit. The profitability case guide works through this kind of problem in full.

Typical restaurant case questions

  • Why are profits falling despite stable sales? (channel mix, food inflation, labour, portion sizes)
  • Should we expand through franchising or company-owned sites?
  • Should we open a delivery-only kitchen?
  • Should a coffee chain take a site in a busy station? (a make an investment question)

What a strong answer sounds like

Weak: "Delivery sales are up 20%, so the delivery partnership is working."
Strong: "Delivery sales are up, but I'd split them into new orders and orders that moved from direct. The moved orders now pay a commission, so profit could be flat or falling even as sales rise."

Common mistakes

  • Counting gross channel sales as growth. Always ask how many orders are new and how many moved from another channel.
  • Ignoring prime cost. Food and labour are most of the cost base, so small percentage changes move profit a lot.
  • Assuming one site predicts all sites. Location drives demand. Test the model against the new site's footfall and rent.
  • Seeing franchising only as lower profit. It is lower profit per site, but much higher return on the chain's capital.

Practise

1. A restaurant serves 250 customers a day at $12, 300 days a year, and keeps a 10% margin. Labour rises from 28% to 31% of sales with nothing else changing. What happens to profit?

Show the answer

Sales: 250 × $12 × 300 = $900k. Profit today: $90k. The margin falls to 7%, so profit is $63k, down 30%.

2. A $30 order costs $9.90 in food and packaging. Through an app charging 30% commission, what does the restaurant keep after food and commission? What if it raises app prices by 15%?

Show the answer

Direct: $30 − $9.90 = $20.10. App: $30 − $9 − $9.90 = $11.10. With 15% higher app prices the order is $34.50: $34.50 − $10.35 − $9.90 = $14.25. Many restaurants charge more on apps for exactly this reason.

3. A chain has $6M to grow. It can open 10 company-owned restaurants like the worked example, or support 40 franchised ones paying a 5% royalty. Which earns more?

Show the answer

Owned: 10 × $216k = $2.16M a year. Franchised: 40 × $1.44M × 5% = 40 × $72k = $2.88M, with most of the $6M still available. Franchising wins on these numbers, if the chain can find good franchisees and protect quality.

Where to practise next

Try the Kettle & Crumb case, where sales grew but profit almost halved, and the Juniper Coffee case on whether to take a new kiosk site. Unit economics explains the single-site logic behind both.
